title: what the bread and the cup are doing
hookLine: a small square of bread and a tiny cup, passed down the row
tomorrow: the three names you say in one breath

lines: A TRAY COMES DOWN THE ROW.
cards: A tray comes down the row. A small square of bread, or a thin wafer. Then a second tray, full of tiny cups: wine in some churches, grape juice in others.
Some people eat right away. Some hold it and wait for everyone. Nobody stops to explain it, and somehow everybody knows what to do.
All of it goes back to one dinner, on the night before Jesus died.

teach.b: The night before he was executed, Jesus ate a Passover meal with his friends. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them: this is my body. Then the cup.
Both times, one request: "this do in remembrance of me." Here's the surprise. Those words aren't only in the Gospels.
A letter Paul wrote to a young church has them too, and it may be older than any Gospel.

His word for remembrance is anamnesis, and many Christians hear more in it than a memory in the head: remembering with your hands, so the thing is present again. That's why the meal has more than one name.
Communion means sharing: one loaf, many people.
The Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks, what he did before he broke the bread. Some churches call it the Lord's Supper. And here churches honestly differ.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine. Many Protestant churches see them as signs, with the remembering at the heart. Others hold careful words of their own.

how: Christians share bread and wine (or grape juice) as Jesus did at the last supper. Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate it at every Mass or Divine Liturgy; Protestant churches share it weekly, monthly or a few times a year, passed down the rows or received at the front; a few groups, such as Quakers, keep no outward meal.

games.q: the night before he died, Jesus takes the bread at the table. what does he do first?
o: passes it to the friend beside him.
games.why: he gives thanks, then breaks it. that thanks is where the name Eucharist comes from.

games.q: put his four moves back in order.

practice: One breath with the bell. Picture a table you've shared: a holiday, a kitchen, a last dinner before someone moved away. See one face at it.
Breathe in. On the way out, let yourself remember them, not just think about them.

wordCard.voice: Communion. Sharing: one loaf, many people, and a meal that remembers. First word on your strand.

orig.note: Greek: sharing, fellowship. Paul's word for the cup and the bread, behind the English communion.

carryVoice: Your line: a meal is a memory. The tray that came down the row was carrying one. See you tomorrow.
